It was both of our opinion that, if the autopilot had been engaged at the start of the encounter, the strength of the wake turbulence would have caused the autopilot to disengage.I notified Departure of the wake turbulence encounter upon check-in, to which they asked for additional information. I described the forcefulness and required actions to counter it, and mentioned that we had no reason to believe there were any injuries or damage.
ASRSN:2236804.s: The pilot flying and co-pilot encountered strong wake turbulence shortly after departing CLT Runway 36C, following an Aircraft Y and an A321. They required frequent manual control inputs to maintain stability but reported no injuries or damage.

ASRSN:2236974.n: During a training flight involving pattern work I was instructed to depart ZZZ's XXR and remain in right closed traffic. I departed behind a Cessna 172 unaware that they are remaining in the pattern. During my crosswind turn to downwind, Tower advised me traffic to follow was the Cessna. However, there was also a Cessna 152 coming in from that general direction to enter in the pattern. I spotted the Cessna 152 and advised 'traffic in sight.' Tower instructed me to follow that traffic. Before my downwind to base turn, I got the instructions that I'm #2, XXR, cleared for the option. I repeated my clearance and still had the Cessna 152 in sight as they were now on final passing my right wing. I turned right base. During my turn to final everything seemed normal, however, within 2.5 miles from the approach end of the runway, ATC asked me if I had the Cessna in sight very exclamatory. I replied 'in sight.' The Cessna 152 I had in sight was departing off of the runway. However I heard the engine of another plane. Apparently, I had cut off the Cessna traffic Tower intended me to follow and we were in very close proximity with each other. I veered right and was told to go around and make right closed traffic at the departure end of the runway. The Cessna 172 I cut off was told to go around and overfly XXL. I take responsibility in the event that occurred as I did not practice what I preach with 'checking final before making the turn to final.' I'm a newly minted CFI and was preoccupied talking about descent, flaps, speeds, etc. during the pattern work. It was an embarrassing moment that showed me how crucial it is to not let teaching preoccupy your fundamental flying habits. When I reflect on the moments leading up to the near miss I think about how the radio calls all made sense. I saw a Cessna on short final, I was #2, XXR cleared for the option. However, technically during that moment I was really #3.Regardless, I spoke to the pilot I cut off on the ground and talked about what had happened. She told me that tower didn't specify which Cessna was to follow as were all in the general vicinity. She had me in sight during my mess up and was able to safely avoid contact since I was in a stable descent and was predictable. Nevertheless, I still take responsibility for not checking final during my turn from base to final.
ASRSN:2236974.s: A newly minted CFI conducting a training flight in a Cessna XXR cut off a Cessna 172 on final approach while preoccupied with instruction. The pilot failed to check final before turning from base, causing a near miss that required both aircraft to go around.

ASRSN:2236990.n: While in cruise noticed a sort of burning or exhaust smell. Grabbed my carbon monoxide detector (electronic) and noticed it was warning me that carbon monoxide was present in the cockpit. Turned off the cabin heat and opened the windows while turning back to home airport. Was at 8500 MSL and about 10 NM from ZZZ. No further issues. Maintenance found large crack in exhaust causing the carbon monoxide leak. The paper detector did not show indications of CO present, the only reason I was able to catch it when I did was due to my electronic portable Carbon Monoxide detector. CO levels would have gotten a lot higher if I did not have an electronic detector. CO detectors should be mandatory for GA aircraft with exhaust shroud style heating sources.
ASRSN:2236990.s: A pilot in cruise at 8500 MSL detected carbon monoxide via an electronic detector, turned off cabin heat, and returned to the airport. Maintenance found a large exhaust crack causing the leak, which the paper detector failed to indicate.

ASRSN:2237001.n: I did not fly for very long or very high, I had received clearances to fly in the area for Day 1 but I thought I got clearances from LAANC to fly on Day 0. Essentially, I mixed up the dates. No incidents or close calls occurred but I did make a mistake flying with clearances in a restricted airspace. I will do better to double check the dates and times of clearances before taking off in the future.
ASRSN:2237001.s: The pilot mistakenly flew in restricted airspace on Day 0 using clearances valid for Day 1 due to a date mix-up. No incidents occurred, and the pilot plans to verify clearance dates and times before future takeoffs.

ASRSN:2237002.n: At about XA:45 on Day 0, I was in the middle of testing out DroneDeploy with a DJI Air 2S in the nearby parking lot of my workplace. I have never used the program before and wanted to do a small test flight so I can understand how to use it before teaching my advanced drone students how it worked. It was about 70% done with the mapping when I suddenly had a low battery warning (30%). Only 6 minutes had passed since I began the operation and the battery that was used initially had a 60% charge. Once the low battery warning started, the drone shot up from 200ft AGL to about 1300ft AGL. During the ascent, I pressed the 'return to home' function on the application on my phone, but it kept climbing to 1300ft. Once it reached that altitude, it went over my location and began to descend back to the ground.I do not know why it decided to climb that high, whether it be a software glitch or interference, but I could have taken steps to research DroneDeploy's software before trying it out blindly on my own. Also, I should've used a fully charged battery.
ASRSN:2237002.s: A drone operator testing a DJI Air 2S with DroneDeploy software experienced an uncommanded climb from 200ft to 1300ft AGL after a low battery warning. The reporter attributed the incident to potential software glitches or interference, noting that using a fully charged battery and researching the software beforehand could have prevented the event.

ASRSN:2237011.n: Aircraft X checked in on frequency, 40 southeast of HLN at 12,000. I asked for a report of 10 miles southeast of HLN. At that point I was going to issue a descent as they exited different MIA (Minimum IFR Altitude) shelves to the SE headed to the HLN VOR for a VOR-A approach. When they reported the 10 miles they reported level at 10,000. I asked them to say again to make sure I heard correctly, they again said they were at 10,000. I then issued a low altitude alert and a climbed to a safe altitude. The aircraft continued without further incident.There continues to be issues with things like this, where HLN in its current state without any type of surveillance and relying and trusting that pilots are always doing the right thing and then they bust an altitude assignment. Change would be recommended to get some kind of display for the sole purpose of situational awareness at the very least.
ASRSN:2237011.s: Air Traffic Control issued a low altitude alert when Aircraft X reported 10,000 feet instead of the assigned 12,000 feet while approaching HLN for a VOR-A approach. The controller directed a climb to a safe altitude, and the reporter attributed the incident to a lack of surveillance at HLN.

ASRSN:2237079.n: Just prior to turn from MNARK encountered wake turbulence that put the aircraft into a 40 degree bank. FO performed upset recovery and the rest of arrival and landing was uneventful. Passengers and flight attendants had been seated well prior to event. After checking on their safety, notified ATC. Autopilot was knocked off as a result of the upset recovery. Dispatch and Chief Pilot notified.
ASRSN:2237079.s: The flight crew encountered wake turbulence near MNARK, causing a 40-degree bank and disengaging the autopilot. The First Officer performed an upset recovery, and the arrival and landing were completed uneventfully with no injuries.

ASRSN:2237157.n: We took off on XXR at ZZZZ. We were bleeds off for max performance. Climbing thru 10 we got Cabin Altitude warning. I continued to fly as the CA ran the Cabin Altitude checklist. We deployed the passenger oxygen mask per the checklist.We requested priority handling leveled off and received vectors back to XXR.We landed a few thousand pounds over weight on XXR. We landed flaps 40 brakes 3. Less than 200 ft a min at touchdown. Turned off at taxiway 1. We then waited for ARF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting) to check the brakes. Once they gave us the all clear. We were towed into the gate.We had medics meet us there for a few passengers that required assistance.Cause: Putting the bleed off checklist back on the checklist. My FO and I had an Improved Performance, bleed off, flap 5 takeoff from ZZZZ. At the gate we briefed the Engine Bleed Off Takeoff Checklist, step by step, and the FO briefed how he would set it up. I also briefed how I would accomplish my after takeoff checklist items. The takeoff was normal, but about the time I completed the after takeoff checklist, The CABIN ALTITUDE warning light illuminated along with the warning horn. I requested priority handling with ATC and started the CABIN ALTITUDE WARNING Checklist on the QRC. The FO and I donned our O2 masks, and silenced the warning horn. At some point I remember seeing the FO turn the packs to Auto. We climbed on the ZZZZZ to about 16,000' (not sure the exact altitude because we were very busy with running the checklist, terrain concerns, and ATC communications). The FO coordinated with ATC, who gave clearance to descend to 12,000'. We wanted to go to 10,000' but were in the 12,100' MSA quadrant. The cockpit was very loud so communication with the FA's (Flight Attendants) was a challenge. My biggest concerns were terrain and getting down to 10,000'. We were given vectors to ZZZZZ1 and were cleared the ILS Z XXR, then cleared the ILS Y XXR, then back to the ILS XXR Z. We did our Descent and Before Landing checklists. At 10,000' I made a PA about returning to the field for the passengers and FA's. I did not accomplish the Non-Routine Landing considerations checklist, instead prioritizing monitoring my Radar Mnm (Minimum) Alts Chart and clarifying MANY clearances with ATC. The FO made a nice approach and an excellent, soft flap 40 landing on XXR. We cleared the runway at taxiway 1, stopped the aircraft and waited for ARFF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting) to check our brake temperatures since we had landed slightly overweight. We were unable to communicate with ARFF at all, so relayed communication through ATC. ATC relayed that ARFF wanted us to shutdown engines, so we complied. Company maintenance came out to the airplane and made the decision to tow us back to the gate. While waiting, we noticed a message on ACARS which indicated a non-standard bleeds/packs configuration was identified. It's a pretty quick climb from 7,297' to 10,000' on the SID, so we did not notice this message during climb-out. We had medical personnel meet us at the airplane to look at one FA who had right ear pain, and one passenger who didn't feel well. Company ops personnel escorted us to airport personnel. We were required to fill out a report and gave them a summary of what happened.Cause: A non-standard bleeds/packs configuration was identified through an ACARS message. When setting the bleeds off takeoff, it's best to go through step by step together before the actual takeoff.
ASRSN:2237157.s: The flight crew performed a bleed-off takeoff from ZZZZ but failed to restore the bleed configuration, causing a cabin altitude warning and oxygen deployment. The aircraft returned to XXR for an overweight landing, and ACARS later confirmed the non-standard bleeds/packs configuration as the cause.

ASRSN:2237163.n: During taxi out to runway XXR the crew was instructed to follow an aircraft proceeding south on taxiway 1. The aircraft was #4 in a line of 4 aircraft holding short of taxiway 2. The line started to move and our instructions from ground were to follow the aircraft in front of us. When it was time to move, I released the parking brake and applied a small amount of thrust to get the aircraft moving. The aircraft did not move. I tried application of the parking brake, cycling it on and off several times, applying thrust each time the brake was off, with the same result. Ground Control queried why we weren't moving and we replied that our brakes were stuck on. At that point, Ground decided to close that section of taxiway 1 and sent several airport utility vehicles out to block the taxiway. I decided to call ZZZ Maintenance on the radio to find out if they had any suggestions on how to release the stuck brake. I tried everything that they suggested, all with the same result. After 30 minutes a maintenance crew arrived at the aircraft and the lead mechanic called me on his cell phone. We tried several different approaches for releasing the pressure on the seized brake, but none were successful. After all efforts were exhausted, we decided to pull airstairs out to the aircraft and bus the passengers back to the terminal. I did make several announcements to the passengers during our delay and the First Officer kept track of our time away from the gate to avoid any DOT violations. The flight attendants did a wonderful job of keeping our passengers comfortable, giving them water, and allowing use of the lavatories. Cause: Mechanical failure. None. First leg of the day, no issues with crewrest, preflight and start normal. Originally given XYL in CPDLC so started both engines. Ground switched to XXR on initial taxi call. Taxiway 3 to 1 to 4, to 2 to follow an aircraft, complied with instructions made RW change briefed close out and holding short of taxiway 2, 3rd in line to turn on to taxiway 2. Parking Brake was set by Captain. Flight control check completed while waiting. Sat in line for about 3-5 mins when the aircraft in front of us and we were cleared to continue taxi on to taxiway 2. Captain released brake applied power but no movement. After a couple tries we notified ATC of our issue and advised we would keep them posted. Contacted local MX (Maintenance) via radio and eventual Maintenance Control via Captains cell phone. Multiple suggestion attempted and did not improve our situation aircraft would not move. We continually updated FAs (Flight Attendants), passengers, ZZZ ops, and ATC. After about 45 mins we opened the tarmac delay app to ensure all requirements were met. After about an hour and a half the plane was deplaned on the taxiway via air stairs and passengers were bussed to the terminal. Shutdown and returned to terminal after all passengers had left.Cause: Maintenance.
ASRSN:2237163.s: During taxi out to runway XXR, the crew could not move the aircraft due to a seized parking brake. After failed maintenance attempts, passengers were deplaned on the taxiway and bussed to the terminal.

ASRSN:2237165.n: Enroute to MIA at FL330, located 70 nm west of EWM VORTAC, the aircraft ECAM reported ADS-B #1 reporting fault. We followed ECAM guidance and changed transponder to #2. Then the ECAM reported ADS-B #1 reporting fault. Then Albuquerque ATC made reports of multiple GPS jamming and ADS-B reporting faults due to military activity in white sands restricted areas. ATC reported jamming to be expected from EWM to PECOS. We reported we had loss ADS-B. Just prior to PECOS the ADS-B returned with no issues the remainder of the flight. We had no GPS jamming throughout the flight. Military activity in restricted areas.
ASRSN:2237165.s: The flight crew en route to MIA at FL330 experienced an ADS-B #1 fault and subsequent loss of ADS-B between EWM and PECOS. Albuquerque ATC attributed the issue to expected GPS jamming from military activity in White Sands restricted areas, though the crew reported no actual GPS jamming.

ASRSN:2237205.n: On final at 2000' at final approach fix, an Aircraft Y crossed under our path at 1,600' causing an RA Maintain". FO disengaged autopilot and maintained altitude until clear of conflict." Responded to a TA/RA for traffic crossing Aircraft Y crossing under at 1600 ft, we were at 2000 ft short final for runway 16L into JAN. Autopilot disconnected and remained level at 2000 until clear of conflict
ASRSN:2237205.s: During final approach to runway 16L at JAN, the crew received a "Maintain" RA when Aircraft Y crossed underneath at 1,600 feet while they were at 2,000 feet. The First Officer disengaged the autopilot and held altitude until the conflict cleared.

ASRSN:2237230.n: While in flight from ZZZ1 to ZZZ, with approximately 15 minutes prior to landing, a passenger's self contained cell phone charger had a thermal runaway and caught fire. The inflight crew notified the flight crew of the situation, and the Captain instructed the inflight crew to extinguish the fire. The Captain requested priority handling with ATC and the flight was cleared to proceed directly to ZZZ. The inflight crew successfully extinguished the fire within seconds by containing the device in the garbage bin of the forward lavatory and then submerging the device with water. The device remained submerged with water in the garbage bin of the forward lavatory for the remainder of the flight. The inflight crew advised the Captain that the fire had been extinguished but the cabin had filled with smoke as a result of the fire. The flight crew performed the Smoke Removal procedure per the QRH. The smoke was only present in the cabin and it did not enter the cockpit at any point. The flight crew was successful in removing the smoke from the cabin. The flight crew received multiple LAV SMOKE ECAM warnings as a result of the smoldering device being placed in the forward lavatory. The Captain issued a briefing to the inflight crew and made a PA to the passengers. Dispatch was notified by ACARS of the situation. The Captain and inflight crew remained in constant communication throughout the remainder of the flight regarding the condition of the device. The flight landed on runway XX in ZZZ, taxied to gate XX and was meet by Crash Fire Rescue personnel who removed the garbage bin containing the submerged device from the aircraft. The passengers deplaned normally through the jet bridge. There were no reported injuries to any passengers or crew as a result of the fire. There was some charring on the seat frame in row 4 ABC and melted plastic on the aisle carpet where the fire took place. The aircraft maintenance log book updated with the appropriate maintenance discrepancies. ZZZ Technician Operations addressed the damage to the aircraft cabin and returned the aircraft into service.
ASRSN:2237230.s: During the approach to ZZZ, a passenger's cell phone charger caught fire, filling the cabin with smoke. The crew extinguished the fire, removed the smoke, and landed safely with no injuries, though minor cabin damage occurred.

ASRSN:2237239.n: Upon taxi we were given [taxiway] 1, 2, 3 hold short of [runway] XXL. The first officer read back the instructions including the hold short. As we approached XXL, ATC told us to follow Aircraft Y or Aircraft Z (can't remember) from the right, monitor tower. We cleared the runway before making the turn on 3, turned the lights on to cross. We checked for traffic which we did not see, anyone on final, and began to cross. Upon reaching the middle of the runway I checked right again and noticed a landing light for XXL. At that point I noticed that there was not enough room to clear the runway due to the lineup of aircraft waiting to takeoff from runway XY. We asked ATC if the aircraft in front of us can move up so we can clear, which they did, however at that point ATC told the aircraft on XXL to go around. At ZZZ, we were cleared to taxi via 1, 2, 3 and to hold short of [Runway] XXL. I copied the instructions on a piece of paper and then read back the instructions, including the hold short detail. After the taxi instructions were read back, we proceeded to taxi along that route, and while under way, we completed the taxi/flight control checks along with the Taxi Checklist. I was performing my duties of monitoring Ground Control while running our checklists. I completed the checklist prior to entering the area of the designated hot spot between Runway XXL and Taxiway 3. We were both heads-up. Around the time of completing the checklist and going heads-up, Ground Control instructed us to follow Aircraft Y ahead and from the right and to monitor Tower. I read those instructions back. Approaching XXL on Taxiway 3, we each cleared the runway, including the final approach path in accordance with our policies and procedures. When I looked to clear the final, I did not see any aircraft. When we reached the middle of the runway we both realized that we couldn't clear it because of the traffic ahead associated with Runway XY. It was at that point that I had a feeling we were not in the correct position and that perhaps we were not in fact cleared to cross XXL. As I queried the Tower to see if they could move the plane up ahead of us, the Captain noticed a small landing light coming from Aircraft Z approaching XXL. Aircraft Z was then instructed to go around. Traffic moved ahead and we proceeded off the runway.
ASRSN:2237239.s: The flight crew crossed Runway XXL while following another aircraft after ATC instructed them to monitor Tower, despite holding short clearance. They realized they could not clear the runway due to traffic on Runway XY and a landing Aircraft Z, which was subsequently instructed to go around.

ASRSN:2237241.n: During cruise with Albuquerque Center we started to hear aircraft stating they were losing GPS capability. Center informed them active GPS jamming was underway and if needed they would provide navigation for them. Within 15 min we in rapid succession lost both of our GPS receivers. We notified ATC and like the other aircraft were told about the jamming underway. We were told our navigation looked good. I checked on the the Nav page and pulled up the position sensors and confirmed both GPS were out but that the IRS and FMS appeared to be working normal. We contacted our dispatcher to inform him what was happening and he could not locate any formal notification that such activity would be taking place and if we needed any assistance to let him know. We started our descent and once handed to El Paso approach notified them that both our GPS was out and would need vectors for our approach for the ILS. After landing both GPS came back online and appeared to be working normal normally. Not sure why the govt/military would jam the GPS receivers of commercial aviation aircraft that rely heavily on that form of navigation without notification being given. Seems a serious potential safety hazard. Other airlines that reported loss of GPS were Company X and Y. Also numerous GA aircraft.
ASRSN:2237241.s: During cruise, the crew lost both GPS receivers due to active jamming reported by Albuquerque Center, while IRS and FMS remained functional. After receiving vectors from El Paso Approach for an ILS landing, GPS systems recovered, though the crew noted the lack of prior notification posed a safety hazard.

ASRSN:2237246.n: Captain got word from ATC (ZAB) that they are doing GPS jamming in that area. There were several commercial flights in the area that completely lost GPS Including the flight I was dispatching. There are no TFR's, MOA, NOTAMs or any reference I can find that this was to be happening. My crew found out when their GPS told them they lost signal.
ASRSN:2237246.s: A dispatcher and crew experienced GPS signal loss during flight due to GPS jamming in the ZAB area, as reported by ATC. No TFRs, MOAs, or NOTAMs existed to indicate this activity, and the crew discovered the issue only when their GPS indicated signal loss.

ASRSN:2237248.n: Encountered clear air turbulence at FL450 just north of COS and east of the Rockies going eastbound. It started as a strong mountain wave that caused loss of 40 kts, and subsequently the autopilot disconnected, and the aircraft gained ~400 feet of altitude and followed by the loss of 500 feet of altitude and moderate turbulence. Denver Center was advised immediately of the event and the gain and loss of the altitude. The duration of the turbulence was less than one minute. Pilot action was to fly the aircraft smoothly, without any abrupt and strong inputs to avoid over-stressing the airplane. Aircraft altitude was recovered and eventually descended to FL410 for a smoother ride. There was no damage or injuries. The rest of the flight was non eventful. Cause: Clear Air Turbulence.Suggestions: There was no report of mountain wave or CAT (Clear Air Turbulence) at the time of the event. However, it's a good idea to be vigilant flying over the Rockies.
ASRSN:2237248.s: The pilot encountered clear air turbulence and a mountain wave at FL450 north of COS, causing autopilot disconnect and altitude deviations. The crew manually stabilized the aircraft, descended to FL410, and reported no injuries or damage.

ASRSN:2237288.n: While performing a touch and go landing, I was somewhat distracted by the fact that I could not lower my flaps from base turn flap setting to full flap setting on final. I elected to continue on with the touch and go landing as I had approximately 7,000 feet of runway ahead of me. Once all wheels were on the ground, I applied full power and then reached for the flap lever to retract the flaps. I inadvertently operated the landing gear lever raising the gear instead. The nose immediately collapsed to the ground causing the propeller to strike the runway multiple times before coming to a stop. There were no injuries. No damage was done to airport property.My dog was my only passenger. I immediately turned the master power off and turned the fuel selector to off and my dog and I exited the aircraft. Fire truck responded to the site as well as law enforcement.The aircraft was jacked up by mechanics and ultimately towed back to my hanger.
ASRSN:2237288.s: During a touch-and-go landing, the pilot inadvertently raised the landing gear instead of retracting flaps after touchdown, causing the nose to collapse and the propeller to strike the runway. The pilot and dog exited safely with no injuries, though the aircraft sustained damage and was later towed to the hangar.

ASRSN:2237301.n: I was a trainee pilot on my first G1000 training flight. The instructor asked me to activate the autopilot once we reached 800 AGL as we climbed out of 47N from RUNWAY 25. We had planned to use the NAV mode and VOR on the CDI to navigate to the SBJ VOR. I had my head down (and I believe the instructor did as well) looking at the G1000 when we got an alert 'Traffic, 1 mile, 1 o'clock, same altitude.' I looked up and saw another aircraft coming towards us. I thought that if pushed too hard on the yoke to maneuver away, I might overpower the AP and activate a runaway trim situation (I completely forgot about the CWS button function to prevent that from happening). I very gently applied pressure on the nose to reduce our rate of climb. The other aircraft turned to the right. We were then alerted to a second plane which was very close behind him and at our 12 o'clock position, also at our altitude and also 1 nm away. At that point, I turned off the autopilot and lowered the nose to avoid the other plane. This all happened in the space of about 45 seconds.What I learned was that it's not a good idea to turn the autopilot on below 2,500 ft AGL in case you have to avoid other pattern traffic (especially for pilots new to the G1000 who haven't gotten that CES muscle memory). I also learned that anyone who puts his/her head down in the cockpit should announce it, just like we do for the positive exchange of controls.
ASRSN:2237301.s: A trainee pilot and instructor in a G1000-equipped aircraft climbing from Runway 25 at 47N received traffic alerts at 800 feet AGL while the autopilot was engaged. The trainee manually maneuvered to avoid two conflicting aircraft, concluding that activating the autopilot below 2,500 feet AGL compromises situational awareness for pattern traffic avoidance.

ASRSN:2237309.n: While taxing with my student and passing another aircraft on an intersecting taxiway, the student unexpectedly added power and too much right rudder. Our wingtip collided with theirs. We had been working on his taxiing throughout the lesson. I was helping him make adjustments and corrections throughout the whole lesson. It was an abrupt movement and there wasn't sufficient time to react. I landed on runway XX, crossed the runway hold markings, stopped and made a clear of active call. While stopped there doing the after landing checklist there was another C172 taxiing down from the other end of the runway. As they passed by us their wingtip struck our wing. Amount of damage is unknown, there is a minimal amount of space between the clear of runway zone and the main taxiway, though avoidable, I could see this being a potential troublesome area for future problems.
ASRSN:2237309.s: A student pilot in a C172 caused two wingtip collisions during taxi and while stopped on the runway due to abrupt power and rudder inputs. The instructor reported insufficient time to react to the student's errors, resulting in unknown damage and highlighting a potential hazard in the limited space between the clear of runway zone and the main taxiway.
